fleet.name: River Fleet
fleet.story: The largest of London's buried rivers. It rises in the Hampstead and Highgate ponds and gives its name to Fleet Street; its lower reaches, the Holbourne, gave Holborn its name. After the Great Fire it became the New Canal, finished in 1680 under Robert Hooke; it was covered over in stages from 1737 to the 1870s and now runs as a sewer. You can still hear it through a grating in Ray Street, Clerkenwell.

tyburn.name: River Tyburn
tyburn.story: Rises at the Shepherd's Well in Hampstead and runs in underground conduits for its whole length, including one beneath Buckingham Palace. Where it split near the Thames it made Thorney Island, on which Westminster Abbey was built. Marylebone Lane still bends along its old bank, and the Tyburn gave its name to the gallows at the end of Oxford Street.

westbourne.name: River Westbourne
westbourne.story: Also called the Kilburn, it gave Bayswater its name. It was dammed in 1730 to make the Serpentine in Hyde Park, which it stopped feeding in 1834 once it had become a sewer. Its pipe still crosses above the platforms of Sloane Square tube station, and it survived the bombing of the station in 1940.

effra.name: River Effra
effra.story: Rises in Upper Norwood and runs under Brixton. By 1821 it was an open sewer below North Brixton, and in 1847 it was arched over as far up as Herne Hill. Bazalgette folded it into his southern sewers. A local story holds that a coffin once fell from a Norwood grave into the buried river and floated to the Thames.

walbrook.name: Walbrook
walbrook.story: The City of London's own stream, now underground. The street called Walbrook follows its lower course, and the valley can still be seen where it meets Cannon Street. The Bank of England and Mansion House stand in the ward named after it.

neckinger.name: River Neckinger
neckinger.story: A short stream from St George's Fields in Southwark to St Saviour's Dock. In 1838 Dickens called Jacob's Island, the district on its tidal ditches, the filthiest of the many places hidden in London, and in 1849 the Morning Chronicle called it the very capital of cholera. In Oliver Twist a branch of it is Folly Ditch.

counters creek.name: Counter's Creek
counters creek.story: Flowed from Kensal Green past Earl's Court to the Thames at Sands End. Its lowest part was turned into the Kensington Canal from 1824, and much of the rest was culverted from 1859 to carry the West London Line. Stamford Bridge, home of Chelsea FC, is named after a bridge over it. Only its tidal mouth, Chelsea Creek, is still open.

hackney brook.name: Hackney Brook
hackney brook.story: Rose near Holloway Road and flowed through Stoke Newington and Hackney to the Lea at Old Ford. Until the late 1830s it was up to 10 metres wide at Stoke Newington. In 1860 Bazalgette's northern high level sewer swallowed it. Builders in the 1860s found flint axes about 200,000 years old on its banks.

moselle.name: Moselle Brook
moselle.story: Rises in Muswell Hill and Highgate and flows through Tottenham. Its stretch by Tottenham High Road and White Hart Lane was covered in 1836, and more culverting from 1906 left it enclosed all the way from Tottenham Cemetery to Pymmes Brook. Muswell Hill shares its name.

peck.name: River Peck
peck.story: A small stream that gave Peckham its name, the homestead of the Peck. It was enclosed in 1823 and still comes to the surface on the west side of Peckham Rye Park before joining Earl's Sluice.

earls sluice.name: Earl's Sluice
earls sluice.story: Runs underground from Ruskin Park on Denmark Hill to the Thames at Deptford Wharf, along the old boundary between Kent and Surrey. Where it crossed the Old Kent Road, Chaucer's pilgrims watered their horses at St Thomas-a-Watering.

stamford brook.name: Stamford Brook
stamford brook.story: A web of small streams between Acton, Hammersmith and Chiswick. By 1900 all six strands had been covered over and turned into sewers. It gave its name to the district and to Stamford Brook tube station.

muswell stream.name: Muswell Stream
muswell stream.story: A headwater of Pymmes Brook below Muswell Hill, listed by Wikipedia among the subterranean rivers as a tributary of a tributary of the Lea. Every metre of it that OpenStreetMap maps is underground.

falcon brook.name: Falcon Brook
falcon brook.story: A south London stream, listed by Wikipedia as one of the subterranean rivers (as Falconbrook). It has no article of its own in the source and is not mapped as a waterway in OpenStreetMap.

wogebourne.name: Wogebourne
wogebourne.story: A stream in south east London, listed by Wikipedia as one of the subterranean rivers. Part of it is still open and part runs in culverts.

graveney.name: River Graveney
graveney.story: A tributary of the Wandle, with its upper course known as Norbury Brook. It runs partly in deep concrete channels; its tributary the Little Graveney Stream was culverted early in the twentieth century and can no longer be seen.

quaggy.name: River Quaggy
quaggy.story: Listed as partly underground. In the 1960s it was put into straight concrete channels to stop flooding; at Chinbrook Meadows the concrete was torn out and the river given back its meanders in 2002, a model for bringing London's rivers back to the surface.
